questions.stem: Market failure exists when:
options: consumers choose not to buy a product that a firm has spent heavily to promote
the price mechanism fails to allocate resources efficiently or fairly
a business fails to make a profit and has to close down within its first year
the price of a good rises sharply because of a fall in supply after a drought
questions.explanation: Market failure means free markets produce too much or too little of something, or produce outcomes society judges unacceptable. A firm closing or a price rising after a supply shock is the market working, not failing.

questions.stem: When a negative externality arises from production, marginal social cost (MSC) is:
options: equal to marginal private cost (MPC), as the cost falls on others
equal to marginal social benefit (MSB) at the market output
greater than marginal private cost (MPC), by the external cost
less than marginal private cost (MPC), by the external cost
questions.explanation: MSC = MPC + external cost, so the full cost to society exceeds what the producer pays. The free market produces where MPC meets demand, which is more than the socially optimal output.

questions.stem: On a graph of a market with a negative production externality, the MSC curve lies above the supply (MPC) curve. Compared with the social optimum, the free market:
options: produces too much at too high a price
produces the optimal quantity at too low a price
produces too much at too low a price
produces too little at too high a price
questions.explanation: Because producers ignore the external cost, the market equilibrium is where MPC meets demand, at a higher quantity and lower price than where MSC meets demand. The gap is overproduction.

questions.stem: When a good creates a positive externality in consumption, such as vaccination, marginal social benefit (MSB) is:
options: equal to marginal private cost (MPC) at every output
equal to zero, as the benefit goes to other people
greater than marginal private benefit (MPB)
less than marginal private benefit (MPB)
questions.explanation: MSB = MPB + external benefit, because others gain when someone is vaccinated. Consumers act only on MPB, so the market underconsumes compared with the social optimum.

questions.stem: On a graph of a market with a positive consumption externality, the MSB curve lies above the demand (MPB) curve. The free market outcome is:
options: a shortage, with demand exceeding supply at the market price
underconsumption, with quantity below the social optimum
overconsumption, with quantity above the social optimum
the social optimum, as supply equals demand
questions.explanation: The market settles where MPB meets supply, at a lower quantity than where MSB meets supply. The market clears, so there is no shortage, but the quantity is too low for society.

questions.stem: A merit good is one that:
options: society judges should be consumed more than the market would provide
society judges should be consumed less than the market would provide
no one can be excluded from using once it has been provided
is provided only by the private sector for profit
questions.explanation: Merit goods such as education and health care tend to be underconsumed, partly because of positive externalities and because people underestimate their benefits. Goods that should be consumed less are demerit goods.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a demerit good?
options: Cigarettes
School education
Public parks
Vaccinations
questions.explanation: Demerit goods, such as tobacco and alcohol, are overconsumed in a free market because consumers underestimate their harm and ignore costs to others. Education, parks and vaccinations are merit or public goods.

questions.stem: Economists argue that pollution of the atmosphere occurs partly because of undefined property rights. This means that:
options: the government owns the air and charges polluters too little
polluting firms own the air and so they can use it as they choose
households own the air and refuse to sell it to polluting firms
no one owns the air, so no one can charge polluters for using it
questions.explanation: Where no one has ownership rights, there is no market price for using the resource, so polluters treat it as free. Defining rights, for example through tradable permits, creates a price.

questions.stem: Fish in international waters are a common-pool resource. They are overfished because they are:
options: non-rival but excludable, so access is sold to the highest bidder
rival but non-excludable, so each fleet takes as much as it can
non-rival and non-excludable, so use by one fleet harms no other
rival and excludable, so only the owner of the fishery can fish there
questions.explanation: A fish caught by one fleet cannot be caught by another (rival), but no one can be prevented from fishing (non-excludable), so each user has an incentive to overuse it. Pure public goods are non-rival.

questions.stem: Which pair of features defines a public good?
options: Non-excludable and non-rival
Excludable and rival
Rival but non-excludable
Excludable but non-rival
questions.explanation: No one can be prevented from benefiting, and one person's use does not reduce what is available to others. Rival but non-excludable goods are common-pool resources.

questions.stem: Private firms will not supply street lighting in a free market mainly because of the free rider problem, which means that:
options: firms that provide the good must give it to some buyers for free
the good is so cheap that no one is willing to pay for it
people can benefit without paying, so firms cannot earn revenue
people refuse to use the good unless it is provided free of charge
questions.explanation: Because users cannot be excluded, each has an incentive to let others pay, so a firm cannot charge enough to cover its costs. Governments therefore provide such goods from taxation.

questions.stem: A large supermarket chain sets prices below cost in one town until a new independent grocer closes, then raises prices again. This is:
options: product differentiation
predatory pricing
collusion
price discrimination
questions.explanation: Predatory pricing uses temporary losses to drive out or deter rivals so that the firm can later charge higher prices. Collusion involves firms agreeing among themselves.

questions.stem: Three cement companies secretly agree to charge the same high price and not to compete for each other's customers. This is:
options: product differentiation, which reduces the elasticity of demand
a natural monopoly, which arises from large economies of scale
collusion, which is illegal cartel conduct in Australia
predatory pricing, which is legal if prices stay above cost
questions.explanation: Agreements to fix prices or share markets are cartel conduct, prohibited under the Competition and Consumer Act 2010 and enforced by the ACCC. They raise prices and cut output, as a monopoly would.

questions.stem: Why does abuse of market power cause market failure?
options: Firms compete so hard that prices fall to the level of marginal cost
Firms cannot exclude non-payers from the goods that they produce
Firms restrict output and raise prices above the competitive level
Firms produce more than consumers want and must cut prices below cost
questions.explanation: A firm with market power can raise profit by producing less and charging more than in a competitive market, so resources are underallocated to the good. Prices at marginal cost are the efficient competitive outcome.

questions.stem: A builder does not tell buyers that an apartment block has known structural defects. This form of asymmetric information is:
options: lack of disclosure
adverse selection
a positive externality
a free rider problem
questions.explanation: Lack of disclosure occurs when a seller withholds information the buyer needs to make a sound decision. Adverse selection is the wider market problem that hidden information can cause, such as only high-risk buyers taking up insurance.

questions.stem: A health insurer cannot tell which applicants are likely to need costly treatment, so it charges everyone an average premium. Healthy people then drop out, and premiums rise further. This is:
options: adverse selection
lack of disclosure
predatory pricing
a common-pool problem
questions.explanation: Adverse selection occurs when hidden information means the buyers who remain are the riskiest, driving prices up and pushing low-risk buyers out. Rules such as lifetime health cover loading try to keep healthier people insured.

questions.stem: Income and wealth inequality is considered a market failure because:
options: markets reward factor ownership, which can leave some people unable to meet basic needs
markets always pay every worker the same wage regardless of their skills or productivity
markets cannot produce enough goods and services to satisfy anyone's basic needs
markets distribute income according to need rather than according to factor ownership
questions.explanation: Market incomes depend on the factors a person owns and sells, so those with few skills or assets may receive very low incomes. Society may judge that outcome inequitable, so government redistributes income.

questions.stem: Social exclusion refers to a situation where people:
options: are prevented by law from owning shares in large companies
cannot take part fully in the economic and social life of the community
choose not to participate in social events because they prefer to work
are excluded from using a good because they have not paid for it
questions.explanation: Low income, poor housing, poor health and lack of access to education or transport can shut people out of work and community life. Exclusion from a good for not paying is a feature of excludable goods.

questions.stem: Why might a government intervene in a market?
options: To prevent prices from changing in every market across the economy
To correct a market failure and improve the allocation of resources
To make every market produce the same quantity of goods and services
To ensure that all businesses make exactly the same level of profit
questions.explanation: Intervention is justified when the market alone over- or under-provides goods, misuses resources or produces inequitable outcomes. It is not meant to equalise profits or freeze prices.

questions.stem: On a demand and supply graph, a per-unit tax on producers of a good with a negative externality shifts:
options: demand left, lowering price but leaving quantity unchanged at the market level
supply left, raising price and reducing quantity towards the social optimum
supply right, lowering price and increasing quantity towards the social optimum
demand right, raising price and increasing quantity towards the social optimum
questions.explanation: The tax raises each unit's cost, moving the supply curve up by the tax and closer to MSC. A tax equal to the external cost would bring output to the social optimum.

questions.stem: A $2 per unit tax is placed on a good with relatively inelastic demand. The price paid by consumers rises from $10 to $11.60. The legal incidence and economic incidence of the tax are:
options: legal on producers; economic $1.60 on consumers and $0.40 on producers
legal on consumers; economic $1.60 on producers and $0.40 on consumers
legal on producers; economic $2.00 on consumers and nothing on producers
legal on producers; economic $0.40 on consumers and $1.60 on producers
questions.explanation: The tax is collected from producers, but consumers pay $1.60 more per unit, and producers keep $11.60 - $2 = $9.60, which is $0.40 less than before. Inelastic demand shifts most of the burden to consumers.

questions.stem: A government subsidy to producers of a merit good is designed to:
options: lower costs, increase supply and raise consumption towards the social optimum
raise costs, reduce supply and cut consumption to the social optimum
raise government revenue that can be spent on other public services
set a minimum price that producers must charge for the merit good
questions.explanation: A subsidy shifts supply right, lowering price and raising quantity to correct underconsumption. Taxes, not subsidies, raise government revenue.

questions.stem: When a government provides a good itself, such as public schools or national defence, this is called:
options: a quantity control
a nudge
direct provision
a price ceiling
questions.explanation: Direct provision is used for public goods and merit goods that markets under-supply, funded from taxation. A price ceiling is a maximum legal price.

questions.stem: A government bans the sale of a harmful chemical pesticide. This form of intervention is:
options: a price floor
direct provision
regulation
a subsidy
questions.explanation: Regulations are laws and rules that require, limit or prohibit actions, such as bans, safety standards and emissions limits. A price floor is a legal minimum price.

questions.stem: The government sets a binding price ceiling on bread below the equilibrium price. On a demand and supply graph, the result is:
options: no effect, as the ceiling is below the equilibrium price
a rise in the equilibrium price to above the ceiling price
a shortage, as quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied
a surplus, as quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded
questions.explanation: A binding ceiling holds price below equilibrium, so consumers want more and producers offer less, creating a shortage. Rationing, queues or black markets may follow. A ceiling above equilibrium would not bind.

questions.stem: The government sets a binding price floor for milk above the equilibrium price. The most likely outcome is:
options: a surplus of milk, which the government may need to buy or dispose of
a shortage of milk, with long queues at shops for the limited supply
no change, because a price floor above equilibrium does not bind
a fall in the price farmers receive below the equilibrium price
questions.explanation: A floor above equilibrium raises quantity supplied and reduces quantity demanded, leaving unsold output. A floor binds only when it is set above the equilibrium price.

questions.stem: A quota limiting the number of taxi licences in a city is an example of:
options: a subsidy
direct provision
a quantity control
a price ceiling
questions.explanation: A quota limits the quantity that can be produced or sold. By restricting supply it tends to raise prices, which is one reason taxi licences became very valuable before ride-sharing.

questions.stem: A government changes the default for organ donation so that people are registered unless they choose to opt out. This is an example of:
options: a nudge
a regulation
a price control
a quantity control
questions.explanation: A nudge changes how a choice is presented to steer behaviour, while leaving people free to choose otherwise. A regulation would require or forbid the behaviour.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a nudge used to address a market failure?
options: Setting a maximum price for fruit sold in canteens
Placing healthy foods at eye level in school canteens
Banning the sale of sugary drinks in all school canteens
Taxing sugary drinks at a fixed rate per litre sold
questions.explanation: Changing the way options are arranged makes the healthier choice easier without banning or taxing anything. A ban is regulation, and a tax or maximum price changes incentives through prices.

questions.stem: Which is a limitation of using a tax to correct a negative externality?
options: A tax cannot change the price that consumers pay for the good
The external cost is hard to measure, so the tax may be set wrongly
A tax always eliminates the externality completely, which is too costly
A tax increases the quantity produced, worsening the externality
questions.explanation: To bring output to the social optimum, the tax must equal the external cost, which is often uncertain. A tax reduces, rather than increases, the quantity produced.

questions.stem: Government failure occurs when:
options: government intervention leads to a less efficient allocation of resources
a government loses an election after introducing an unpopular policy
a government is unable to borrow money to fund a budget deficit
government spending on public goods is higher than in the previous year
questions.explanation: Intervention can make outcomes worse through poor information, unintended consequences, high administrative costs or political influence. Losing an election is a political outcome, not an economic concept.

questions.stem: An industry association lobbies the government for a subsidy that raises its members' profits but provides no wider benefit to society. This is an example of:
options: rent-seeking behaviour
a positive externality
the free rider problem
adverse selection
questions.explanation: Rent-seeking is using resources to gain economic benefits through the political process rather than by producing value. It can lead to interventions that misallocate resources, a form of government failure.

questions.stem: A city introduces a binding rent ceiling to make housing more affordable. Several years later, fewer rental properties are available and many are poorly maintained. This best illustrates:
options: predatory pricing by large landlords
an unintended consequence of a price control
a positive externality from new housing
the free rider problem in rental housing
questions.explanation: A ceiling below equilibrium reduces landlords' returns, so over time supply falls and maintenance declines, worsening the shortage the policy aimed to ease. This is a classic case of government failure.

questions.stem: A government hands out free fishing licences with no limit on catch to support a coastal town. The fishery is soon depleted. This shows that:
options: poorly designed intervention can worsen a common-pool problem
public goods are always overproduced when governments intervene
a price floor creates a surplus of fish in the market
market power allows one firm to restrict the catch of fish
questions.explanation: Encouraging more fishing without limits increases overuse of a rival, non-excludable resource. Quotas or tradeable catch rights would address the underlying problem.

questions.stem: Which statement about using regulation rather than a tax to reduce pollution is correct?
options: Regulation always reduces pollution at a lower total cost than a tax
Regulation raises government revenue that can fund environmental programs
Regulation works through the price mechanism by changing relative prices
Regulation sets clear limits but gives no incentive to cut below them
questions.explanation: A standard sets a clear limit, but once firms comply they gain nothing from cutting further, and it may impose the same rule on firms with very different costs. Taxes raise revenue and work through prices.

questions.stem: A negative externality is best described as:
options: a benefit gained by third parties who are not part of the transaction
a cost paid by the buyer of a good in addition to its market price
a tax imposed by the government on goods that harm consumers
a cost imposed on third parties who are not part of the transaction
questions.explanation: Externalities are spillover effects on people outside a transaction; negative ones are costs, such as noise or pollution. A spillover benefit is a positive externality.

questions.stem: Which is an example of a merit good?
options: Tobacco
Gambling
Alcohol
Health care
questions.explanation: Health care is underconsumed in a free market relative to its benefits to individuals and society, so governments subsidise or provide it. Tobacco, gambling and alcohol are demerit goods.
